1107.title: A covenant (CCC 1601; 1644)
1107.hook: marriage as a lifelong covenant of partners
1107.howItsDone: At a Catholic wedding the bride and groom freely exchange their consent and vows before a priest or deacon and witnesses, and the Church regards the couple themselves as the ministers of the sacrament.

segments.voice: Yesterday, celibacy, and the married priests of the Eastern Churches. Your line was two traditions. Now, from the priesthood to marriage.

A phone contract has a term. A lease has an end date. A gym membership lasts until you find the cancel button. Contracts are useful: they say what each side owes, for how long, and what happens if someone doesn't deliver. Then, on a Saturday afternoon, two people stand at the front of a church and promise something with no end date and no exit clause: for better, for worse, in sickness and in health. Whatever that is, it's not a phone plan.
screen: `A TERM. AN END DATE.` → `NO END DATE.` → `NOT A PHONE PLAN.`

segments.voice: The Catechism opens its teaching on marriage with this word: covenant. Marriage, it says, is a covenant by which a man and a woman form a partnership of the whole of life, ordered to the good of the spouses and to the procreation and education of children. Between the baptized, Christ raised it to the dignity of a sacrament. What makes a covenant different? Some teachers put it this way. A contract trades things: money for a service, rent for a room. A covenant gives persons. A contract says, I'll do this if you do that. A covenant says, I am yours. Covenants run through the Bible: God makes them with Noah, with Abraham, with Israel at Sinai, and the prophets reach for marriage to describe them, God as a faithful husband who doesn't walk away, even when his people do. So calling marriage a covenant borrows the language of God's own faithfulness. Genesis, in the Douay-Rheims: "Wherefore a man shall leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they shall be two in one flesh." The love of the spouses, the Catechism says, by its nature asks for unity and indissolubility, a partnership for the whole of life, and for faithfulness, rooted in God's own fidelity and Christ's love for the Church. That's why a Catholic wedding has vows, not terms. The couple give consent freely, before witnesses. And in the Latin Church, Catholic teaching says the couple are themselves the ministers of the sacrament: the priest or deacon witnesses, and the two give it to each other.
screen: `A PARTNERSHIP OF THE WHOLE OF LIFE.` · `A CONTRACT TRADES THINGS. A COVENANT GIVES PERSONS.` · `TWO IN ONE FLESH.` · `UNITY, FAITHFULNESS, FOR LIFE.`

1108.title: The domestic church (CCC 1655–1658)
1108.hook: the family home as a little church
1108.howItsDone: Catholic families may say grace before meals, pray at bedtime with children, keep a crucifix or holy images at home, and mark feasts and seasons such as Advent and Lent around the table.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a covenant: marriage as a gift of persons, a partnership of the whole of life. Your line was covenant, not contract.

Someone says grace, fast, before the food goes cold. It's a weeknight: homework at one end of the kitchen table, a laptop at the other, a pot on the stove. A toddler joins in late with the amen. On a shelf above the sink there's a small crucifix, a palm leaf from last spring gone brown, and a photo of a grandmother who died. It doesn't look like a holy room. The Catechism gives it a holy name all the same.

segments.voice: The Catechism starts in the Acts of the Apostles, where more than once someone comes to believe together with their whole household. The jailer at Philippi, shaken by an earthquake, is baptized that same night with all his family. Lydia, a seller of purple cloth, is baptized with her household. Paul and Silas tell the jailer that if he believes in the Lord Jesus, he and his house will be saved: the promise is made to a household. These homes, the Catechism says, became islands of Christian life in a world that didn't yet believe. Then it takes a phrase from the Second Vatican Council: the family as the domestic church. Ecclesia domestica. Not a metaphor for something lesser. The home is where children first hear the faith, from their parents, by word and example, and where a vocation, any vocation, is first noticed. The Catechism calls it the first school of Christian life. There you learn endurance and the joy of work, love between brothers and sisters, and generous forgiveness, again and again. There the family prays together and offers its life to God. So the ordinary things count: grace before meals, a blessing at bedtime, a fight made up before sleep. And the Catechism doesn't forget people without a family nearby: the single, the widowed, people far from home. The Church's doors must be open to them, it says. No one is without a family in this world: the Church is a home and family for everyone, especially those who labor and are burdened.
screen: `HOUSEHOLDS IN ACTS.` · `ECCLESIA DOMESTICA.` · `THE FIRST SCHOOL OF CHRISTIAN LIFE.` · `NO ONE WITHOUT A FAMILY.`

1109.title: Sacramentals (CCC 1667–1673)
1109.hook: holy water, blessings, medals, ashes: signs that prepare us for grace
1109.howItsDone: Catholics bless themselves with holy water on entering a church, wear blessed medals or scapulars, receive ashes on Ash Wednesday, and ask priests to bless homes, objects and people.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the domestic church: the home as a little church, and the Church as a home for everyone. Your line was a little church.

At the back of a glove box, behind the registration and a tire gauge, a small medal of Saint Christopher on a chain, gone dull. Nobody remembers who put it there. On a windowsill at home, a plastic bottle shaped like the Virgin Mary, half full of water. A farmer asks a priest to bless his tractor. On Ash Wednesday, strangers on a subway car share the same gray smudge. None of these is a sacrament. All of them are something, and the Catechism has a word for that something.
screen: `A MEDAL IN THE GLOVE BOX.` → `WATER IN A BOTTLE ON THE SILL.` → `A GRAY SMUDGE ON A FOREHEAD.`

segments.voice: Sacramentals, the Catechism says, are sacred signs that bear a likeness to the sacraments: holy water, blessings, medals, ashes, the sign of the cross, a blessed candle. The difference matters. Catholic teaching holds that the sacraments were instituted by Christ and give grace through the action itself. Sacramentals were instituted by the Church. They don't give grace the way a sacrament does; they prepare a person to receive grace and cooperate with it, working through the prayer of the Church. They clear the ground. A sacramental takes an ordinary moment, walking into a building, starting a car, falling asleep, and opens it toward God. For well-disposed believers, the Catechism says, almost every event of life can be made holy this way. Among sacramentals, blessings come first, and Scripture has them too. In Numbers, God gives Aaron's family words to bless the people with. In the Douay-Rheims they begin: "The Lord bless thee, and keep thee." Blessings of people, meals, objects, places. And a detail worth keeping: every baptized person, the Catechism says, is called to be a blessing, and to bless. Some blessings belong to bishops and priests, but parents can bless their children, and a family can bless its table. One more thing it keeps clear: the power isn't in the water or the metal by itself. A medal isn't a charm. It works, Catholic teaching says, through the Church's prayer and the faith of the person who uses it.
screen: `SIGNS THAT RESEMBLE THE SACRAMENTS.` · `THEY PREPARE FOR GRACE.` · `THE LORD BLESS THEE, AND KEEP THEE.` · `NOT A CHARM.`

Then let one ordinary part of your day come to mind, the drive, the desk, the dishes, and picture it marked the same way.

1110.title: Popular piety (CCC 1674–1676)
1110.hook: processions, pilgrimages, relics, rosaries: the faith of ordinary people
1110.howItsDone: Catholics keep popular devotions such as the rosary, the stations of the cross, novenas, pilgrimages to shrines, and processions on saints' feast days, organized by parishes and families alongside the Mass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sacramental: holy water, blessings, medals, ashes, signs that prepare for grace. Your line was small holy things.

A brass band plays slowly down a narrow street. Behind it, a statue of Mary sways on the shoulders of men in their Sunday shirts, sweating and grinning. Old women walk barefoot behind them with beads in their hands. Kids run alongside, eating ice cream. Someone pins a bill to the statue's ribbon. No priest directs the band, and no book of rites tells anyone to bring the ice cream. And yet it's prayer, loud and public, carried by the people themselves. The Catechism makes room for exactly this.
screen: `A BRASS BAND, A SWAYING STATUE.` → `BAREFOOT, WITH BEADS.` → `PRAYER CARRIED BY THE PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Besides the liturgy and the sacraments, the Catechism says, the faith of Christian people finds expression in many forms of piety. Then it names them: the veneration of relics, visits to sanctuaries, pilgrimages, processions, the stations of the cross, religious dances, the rosary, medals. Religious dances, right there in the Catechism. The list shows faith spilling into streets, kitchens, hillsides and festivals, in the shape of each people's own culture. The Bible has its pilgrims. In Luke, Mary and Joseph go up to Jerusalem for the Passover, and the boy Jesus goes with them. The Psalms include songs that tradition says were sung on the road up to the Temple. Walking toward God with a crowd is an old habit. Then the Catechism sets a frame. These devotions extend the liturgical life of the Church; they don't replace it. They grow out of the Mass and lead back toward it. A procession for a saint's feast can end at the church door. The rosary walks through the life of Christ that the liturgy celebrates. And last, discernment. The Catechism asks pastors to support popular piety, and also to purify and correct it where needed. It quotes bishops from Latin America who called the people's piety a storehouse of values, answering life's questions with Christian wisdom: holding together the divine and the human, body and spirit, faith and homeland, and finding reasons for joy even in a hard life. Popular piety, in that view, isn't a lesser faith for people who don't read theology. It's theology walking down the street.

1111.title: Christian funerals (CCC 1680–1690)
1111.hook: the Church accompanies the dead with hope and commends them to God
1111.howItsDone: A Catholic funeral usually includes a vigil or wake, a funeral Mass with the coffin received at the church door and covered with a white pall, and a final commendation before burial, with prayers at the graveside.

segments.voice: Yesterday, popular piety: processions, pilgrimages, rosaries, the faith of ordinary people. Your line was the people's faith.

The coffin comes in at the back of the church, and the priest meets it at the door. He sprinkles it with water, the way water was poured on this person at baptism, long ago, maybe in this same building. A white cloth is spread over the wood; nobody can tell whether the one inside was rich or poor. The family walks behind, eyes down. By the altar burns the candle that was lit at Easter. Every gesture is saying something.
screen: `MET AT THE DOOR.` → `WATER, AS AT BAPTISM.` → `A WHITE CLOTH, A CANDLE.`

segments.voice: The Catechism begins with hope. For a Christian, death is seen in the light of Christ's death and resurrection. Jesus tells Martha, in John, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am the resurrection and the life: he that believeth in me, although he be dead, shall live." That's the key the whole funeral is played in. It doesn't give the dead a sacrament, the Catechism says. It expresses the Church's communion with them, gathers the living, and proclaims eternal life. Then the shape of the rite. First, the greeting. In the rite, the community welcomes the person one last time, at the door, as it once did at baptism, and speaks words of comfort and hope to the family. Second, the word. Scripture is read, even in grief, because the Church holds that God's word speaks into death too. Wisdom, in the Douay-Rheims: "the souls of the just are in the hand of God." Third, the Eucharist. The Church offers the Mass for the one who has died; Catholics believe this prayer helps them, and that the bond between the living and the dead isn't broken. Fourth, the farewell. The Church commends the person to God: the community's last goodbye before the body goes to the grave. A commendation is a handing over: here is someone we loved; we place them in your hands. Today also closes Part Two, How we celebrate, which ran from the liturgy and the sacraments to sacramentals, devotions and this farewell: from the font to the grave.
screen: `DEATH IN THE LIGHT OF THE RESURRECTION.` · `THE GREETING AT THE DOOR.` · `THE WORD AND THE EUCHARIST.` · `THE FAREWELL: COMMENDED TO GOD.`

And if grief has taken you somewhere dark, or you don't want to be alive, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

1112.title: Called to beatitude (CCC 1716–1729)
1112.hook: the beatitudes describe the happiness God wants for us
1112.howItsDone: Catholics hear the beatitudes from Matthew 5 read at Mass, and the Catechism places them near the start of its teaching on the moral life, before the commandments.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Christian funerals: the Church hands the dead over to God. Your line was commended to God. Now a new part begins: how Catholics live.

The Catechism's part on how Catholics live could have started with a list of rules. It doesn't. It turns to a mountain, a crowd, and one word said again and again: blessed. Blessed are the poor in spirit. Blessed are the meek. Blessed are they that mourn. Before any instruction about what to avoid, Jesus describes people who are, in his word, blessed. Some don't look it at all: the grieving, the hungry and thirsty, the persecuted. A surprise about who is happy.
screen: `NOT A LIST OF RULES.` → `BLESSED, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` → `THE GRIEVING, THE PERSECUTED.`

segments.voice: Back on day three hundred twelve, you met the beatitudes as a portrait of Jesus. The Catechism calls them the heart of Jesus's preaching. In the Douay-Rheims the first reads: "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." Some readers hear blessed as happy, and the Catechism comes close: the beatitudes, it says, answer the natural desire for happiness, a desire that comes from God, placed in the heart to draw people to himself. Saint Augustine, quoted there, asks God: how is it that I seek you? Because in seeking you, I seek the happy life. So morality here doesn't start with what's forbidden. It starts with what a person wants most, and the claim that God wants it for them too. Then the beatitudes turn that wanting around. True happiness, the Catechism says, isn't found in riches or comfort, fame or power, or any human achievement, however useful. It names the goal: the coming of the kingdom, the vision of God, entering into God's rest. "Blessed are the clean of heart: for they shall see God." And the beatitudes show the face of Jesus Christ. They describe him first, the poor one, the meek one, the one who mourned, and then the happiness held out to anyone who follows. So the question shifts: not only what am I allowed to do, but what am I made for. The beatitudes put decisive choices in front of a person, and everything in this part of the book, the commandments included, comes after that.
screen: `THE HEART OF JESUS'S PREACHING.` · `A DESIRE FOR HAPPINESS, FROM GOD.` · `NOT RICHES, FAME OR POWER.` · `THE FACE OF CHRIST.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE THE CLEAN OF HEART.`

segments.voice: Start with the surface wants, a quieter week, a bit more money, and let them go by. Then ask underneath: if I had all of those, what would I still want? Keep asking until you reach something you can't buy, to be known, to be at peace, to love someone well, and if you pray, hold that desire up to God; if you don't, just stay with it.

1113.title: What makes an act good (CCC 1750–1756)
1113.hook: the act itself, the intention and the circumstances
1113.howItsDone: Catholic moral teaching weighs an act by its object, its intention and its circumstances, and some Catholics use those three in an examination of conscience before confession.

segments.voice: Yesterday, called to beatitude: the moral life begins with the happiness a person is made for. Your line was made for happiness.

Sunday, the collection basket comes down the pew. Three envelopes go in. The first is from a woman who heard the parish is helping a family that lost its home in a fire. The second is from a man who folds his so the person beside him can see how thick it is. The third is from a woman who lost her job last month and gave anyway, less than she used to. From the back of the church, all three look identical. What makes an act good?
screen: `THREE ENVELOPES, ONE BASKET.` → `SAME ACT FROM THE BACK PEW.` → `WHAT MAKES IT GOOD?`

segments.voice: The Catechism answers with three things, which it calls the sources of morality. First, the object: what is actually chosen. Giving money, telling the truth, telling a lie. Reason looks here first, and some acts are wrong whatever the reason behind them. Second, the intention: why, the end a person has in view. One intention can run through a whole string of actions, and one action can carry several intentions. Third, the circumstances: who, where, when, how much, under what pressure. Then how they fit, and the Catechism is plain. A good intention can't make a bad act good. Its example is lying: even to help a neighbor, a lie is still a lie. In one short phrase: the end does not justify the means. It goes the other way too: a bad intention can spoil a good act. The example comes from Jesus, about giving alms to be seen. In the Douay-Rheims: "sound not a trumpet before thee." The man folding his envelope for the pew is doing a good thing for a hollow reason. Circumstances can make an act more or less good, more or less serious; fear, for instance, can lessen a person's responsibility. But they can't turn a wrong act into a right one. So a good act needs all three together: a good object, a good intention, fitting circumstances. And the third envelope? Thinner, maybe. But a lost job and a tight month add weight to that gift.
